Yellow jacket wasp (queen). I found it on the window of an outside staircase, put my finger up to it, and it walked on and started lapping up my sweat. I presume it did so partially because the temperature was so hot, and it had been stuck on the window for a while (basically a big insect trap), hence the wasp might be thirsty (and I was quite sweaty). It stayed on my hand for several minutes, drinking and frequently cleaning itself. 

Then wasp systematist Lynn Kimsey walks by, says "Oh, made a new friend?" and takes a closer glance at the wasp on my hand, then says "Yup, that's a queen." So, yeah, apparently I fed a queen yellow jacket with my sweat. No stinging involved whatsoever. 

Here is a video of it walking on my hand, then flying off; unfortunately, I was too late in recording video to capture its drinking: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m_9iTJR53lw

Behavior series

Photo 2:  The Ant Wants Some Too
I didn't even see the ant until I was processing my photos.  My guess is that it wanted some of the food too.  Can you see it on the piece of corn at the bottom?
Photo 3:  Full Profile View Of The Southern Yellowjacket

description: This organism is oval-shaped with beady, black eyes. Antennae is present in this organism. The wings of this organism are greater than the body itself, which suggests this as an important body structure. The body has a yellow and black striped pattern, which is characteristic of the Yellowjackets from the Vespula genus. The top of the body has a horizontal, alternating striped pattern, while the rest of the body has a vertical, alternating striped pattern. According to the Washington Nature Mapping website, yellowjackets have "yellow markings on the front of the head and yellow banding around the abdomen. The face is primarily yellow with dark eyes. description:
This nest stung, 5 times that I personally know of (me).  Right at the edge of a trail in Lewis Creek Park, I was looking to take a photo of something and happened to stand right near it, and this displeased at least one of the nest members.  It was not long before sunset, but I stayed until dusk getting other park visitors to detour around it... especially given a number of people were jogging and likely to jar it (perhaps not getting stung themselves, but making the wasps more prone to go after anybody passing soon after).  I called and left the ranger messages and they blocked the trail early the nest morning until the nest could be disposed of (which I don't like being a part of, but I'd hate for somebody to have serious sting issues, or worse, a bad allergic reaction).  Had it been on my property I would leave it and study them.

Was a bit surprised that Forest Yellowjacket wasn't even one of the suggestions here, although the trail was not in the forest, it was under an oak tree within 20' of the edge of the forest.

Guessing it may be "Vespula alascensis".

Source: 9/2: IMG_7565x, 63x, 64x; 9/3: 7665x (broader nest entrance only)

description: The eastern yellow jacket or eastern yellowjacket is a wasp found in eastern North America. Although most of their nests are subterranean, they are often considered a pest due to their nesting in recreational areas and buildings. From the order of Hymenopterans, and family of Vespidae, unlike the nests of bees, the nests of yellowjackets contain no honey or pollen. Yellowjacket larvae eat meat and carbohydrate rich foods gathered by the workers. In this regard, yellowjackets are beneficial because they kill many caterpillars and beetles that are pests in our gardens. By late summer and early autumn, colonies may contain thousands of workers and are often about the size of a football. Under extraordinary circumstances, some nests may persist for more than one year and reach gigantic proportions. There are reports of monster yellowjacket nests in southern states reaching the size of a “Volkswagen Beetle”.  The workers and males lack free spots on the abdomen. Wide anchor-shaped black marking with narrow base on first abdominal tergite is diagnostic. Queens have free black spots on abdominal tergites, but show the distinctive anchor-shaped marking on T1 rather than the diamond-shaped marking of V. germanica. Xanthic individuals do occur, more commonly in southern part of range, and these can sometimes have yellow marks on the mesoscutum. They can commonly be found in forests, meadows and forest edges, including urban and suburban environments. Like in all Vespula, colonies are normally subterranean, or sometimes at ground level in stumps and fallen logs. In deciduous forest, nest entrances frequently situated under tree roots or adjacent to logs on the ground. This particular yellowjacket was found in the leaf piles of Reedy Creek. The leaves were surrounded by woodland.

description: Vespula squamosa, the southern yellowjacket, is a social wasp. This species can be identified by its distinctive black and yellow patterning and orange queen. These yellowjackets are typically found in eastern North America, and its territory extends as far south as Central America. These insects belong to the order Hymenoptera and family Vespidae. The worker yellow jackets are sized at 9.5–11.0 mm, the females are sized at 15.0–16.5 mm and males at 12.5 mm. These were identified with  all castes possessing conspicuous yellow longitudinal stripes on the mesoscutum, a trait shared with the closely-related allopatric V. sulphurea but no species within its range. The workers and males have similar abdominal patterns, with no free spots and an unusual pair of lateral yellow stripes through the black basal band of the second tergite. description: This bee was identified as an Eastern Yellowjacket by its striking yellow and black striped body. Though visually similar to the European Paper Wasp, it was distinguished by its thicker body and black antennae, as paper wasps are thinner with orange antennae. Finally, the individual was about 1.5 cm long, which is typical of the species as yellowjackets range from about 1.2-1.8 cm. Because Eastern yellowjackets consume other insects during their larval stage, they are considered secondary consumers. Like other bees, the life cycle of the Eastern Yellowjacket includes an egg, larval, pupal, and adult stage. Eggs are hatched by a queen and remain as larvae for about two weeks before going through a pupal stage and finally emerging as adults. This individual was likely an adult, as it was spotted on a plant away from its nest. Like other social bees, the life cycle of yellowjackets can also be expressed from the viewpoint of the colony rather than the individual. Queens awaken from hibernation in the spring months, locate a new nesting site, and begin to lay eggs. These eggs become worker bees that help take care of the colony. Later in the summer, probably about the time of this sighting, new queens and males are produced, mate, and new queens then hibernate before forming new colonies in the spring. This bee was also most likely a worker female, as the yellow and black bands on its back lacked the polka-dot pattern of the queen and the black bands did not gradually decrease in thickness as they do for males. Eastern yellowjackets are found in habitats such as meadows, fields, and forests, but are also common to urban and suburban areas. Other organisms that may inhabit these areas are trees, grasses, other insects, birds, skunks, raccoons, and deer. This individual was found in a meadow area with lots of flowering plants. A potential predator of the Eastern Yellowjacket is the Striped Skunk (Mephitis mephitis nigra), while a source potential prey are flies like the House Fly (Musca domestica). A potential competitor of the species is the Bald-faced Hornet (Dolichovespula maculata).

They are secondary consumers feeing on insects like honeybees that they then feed to their larvae. Raccoons are a common predator of Yellowjackets and will go after their nests. They could. description:
Eastern Yellowjacket
•	Trophic level: Primary/secondary consumer
•	Description: Recognizable pest. Small, bee-like insect with bright black-and-yellow markings on head, thorax, and abdomen, with yellow legs. Easily Distinguishable from a bee by behavior, often buzzing around people and food and uninterested in flowers. Similar to the Bald-faced Hornet, which is larger and lacks any yellow coloration.
•	Life Cycle: New colonies are created in the spring by a select number of queens who survive the winter after mating and subsequent hibernation. The queen lays eggs in a newly established nest, and once hatched these workers continue construction. Individuals, derived from the queen, undergo development within the nest, and social structure is similar to that of other eusocial insects. Hives die off in the fall, excluding queens. 
•	Stage: The observed individual is an adult. 
•	Sex: The observed individual is most likely a worker and therefore a female.
•	Habitat: Nests are built in the ground in forests or suburban areas. 
•	Predator: Raccoon
•	Prey: European Earwig
•	Competitor: European Paper Wasp

Temperature (f): 85 degrees
Weather Conditions: hot, humid


During my first observation today, I saw 2 German Yellowjackets. The Yellowjackets were relatively calm and stayed on the purple flowering bush (glossy abelia) for most of the time. One important point to note is that the area just had sprinklers go off, so it was quite damp on the grass in front of my site.

Temperature (f): 79 degrees
Weather Conditions: Slightly windy,
Perfect evening weather


Today was slightly abnormal in comparison with my previous observation days. There were only 2 German Yellowjackets and they seemed very anxious. They would not stay still, which made taking my pictures slightly difficult. Similar to other days, the Yellowjackets spent most of their time on the right purple flowering bush (glossy abelia); although they did move to the large tree as well. Overall, my observation site has not changed at all since beginning my project. But one thing to note is that the area near my site was very dry today because of a lack of rain and sprinkler water in recent days.

description:
Temperature (f): 73 degrees
Weather Conditions: cool, borderline chilly, sun-setting


Similar to my observations on 9-21-2020, there were very few pollinators at my site. I spotted 2 German yellowjackets and 1 Coarse-backed Red Paper Wasp; all of them seemed uneasy. This observation leads me to believe that as we move further into fall, and thus the sun sets earlier, the insects that interact with my site may become less active earlier in the evening. This is possibly why I am not seeing as many pollinators when I make observations later in the day as opposed to in the morning or afternoon.

Habitat: This organism was found at Edward Medard park in Turkey Creek, FL. The Southern YellowJackets are most commonly found in Eastern North America, however range to the south of Central America. These insects tend to stay in areas with a warmer climate.

description:
Dozens of wasps on a circular trough filled with pond scum. They appeared to be drinking. 

Western Yellowjacket (Vespula pensylvanica) is native across the western half of North America. They are both carnivore and herbivore. V. pensylvanica can usually be differentiated from other species of social wasps in the genus Vespula by the continuous yellow ring (often referred to as an eye-loop) present around each eye. The eye-loop is not always present. Though few females lack this distinguishing characteristic, males often do not have the eye-loop. In such cases, V. pensylvanica can be identified by a spotted mark on the frons below the antenna, a slender aedeagus, and a denser apical region of tergum 7. The fore wing length ranges from 8.5-10.5 mm for workers, 12.5-14.5 mm for females, and 12.5-14.0 mm for males.
Western yellowjackets build large nests made of wood fibers, enclosed in a hexagonal paper envelope with a small 10– to 30-cm entrance tunnel at the bottom. Nests are usually found 10–15 cm below ground or in other dark cavities, such as rodent burrows.https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/61355-Vespula-pensylvanica

Western Yellowjacket (Vespula pensylvanica) is native across the western half of North America. They are both carnivore and herbivore. V. pensylvanica can usually be differentiated from other species of social wasps in the genus Vespula by the continuous yellow ring (often referred to as an eye-loop) present around each eye. The eye-loop is not always present. Though few females lack this distinguishing characteristic, males often do not have the eye-loop. In such cases, V. pensylvanica can be identified by a spotted mark on the frons below the antenna, a slender aedeagus, and a denser apical region of tergum 7. The fore wing length ranges from 8.5-10.5 mm for workers, 12.5-14.5 mm for females, and 12.5-14.0 mm for males.
Western yellowjackets build large nests made of wood fibers, enclosed in a hexagonal paper envelope with a small 10– to 30-cm entrance tunnel at the bottom. Nests are usually found 10–15 cm below ground or in other dark cavities, such as rodent burrows.https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/61355-Vespula-pensylvanica

Visual description: This wasp was approximately two inches long. It had black and yellow coloration and it’s antennas were black. The waist was very slim and a black triangle shape was on its thorax. The abdomen had a pattern of two black dots with a diamond shape between them running down to the stinger. 

Defining characteristics: This species is a protostome that usually has a diamond shaped black mark  on the dorsal side. The adults have a distinct segmented body with a thin waist. They are hairless and have elongated wings that fold laterally against their body when at rest. The stinger does not detach, meaning that they can sting multiple times. If it is killed or attached it will release pheromones to alert other yellow jackets to come help. 

Habitat: This wasp was located in my back yard. This species is widely distributed in the northern hemisphere. It tends to nest in various environments since they adapt well. They live in rural, suburban and urban areas.

Western Yellowjacket (Vespula pensylvanica) is native across the western half of North America. They are both carnivore and herbivore. V. pensylvanica can usually be differentiated from other species of social wasps in the genus Vespula by the continuous yellow ring (often referred to as an eye-loop) present around each eye. The eye-loop is not always present. Though few females lack this distinguishing characteristic, males often do not have the eye-loop. In such cases, V. pensylvanica can be identified by a spotted mark on the frons below the antenna, a slender aedeagus, and a denser apical region of tergum 7. The fore wing length ranges from 8.5-10.5 mm for workers, 12.5-14.5 mm for females, and 12.5-14.0 mm for males.
Western yellowjackets build large nests made of wood fibers, enclosed in a hexagonal paper envelope with a small 10– to 30-cm entrance tunnel at the bottom. Nests are usually found 10–15 cm below ground or in other dark cavities, such as rodent burrows.https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/61355-Vespula-pensylvanica

description:
The organism was approximately an inch long, I don’t know exactly as I didn’t get close enough to measure it. It had 3 clear body segments with the rear segment being the biggest and wings as well as antennas. Its coloration was very unique with a pattern of alternating yellow and black. The organism also had 6 legs. None of the reproductive structures were visible. 
I identified this organism to be a yellowjacket. Its higher taxon is Hexapoda, and I'm confident it is Hexapoda due to several key characteristics I noticed about it. First the organism has 6 legs hence the name Hexa or six. Second the organism has 3 body segments which are indicative of the group Hexapoda. 
This organism was observed in a wet land area that bordered a river. It was found actively flying around in the morning and landed on a wooden railing that belonged to a bridge that crossed over wetland. The area around was densely vegetated with many large trees that extended out of the water. 
The southern yellowjacket is found in the Americas ranging from Texas as its northern boundary all the way to South America. 
The organism was found very active in the morning time.

description:
1) Description: Vespula squamosa or the Southern Yellowjacket in the picture above is about half of an inch long with black and yellow stripes along its body. The yellow stripes tend to be larger than the black stripes. Their wings are about the same size as their body or slightly longer.  When not flying their wing lay flat on their thorax. This Southern yellowjacket's antenna is flexible due to the fact that it pressed in the wood.  
2) Range: Southern Yellowjackets can be found in the Eastern United States, a little towards the mid states and Mexico's center. 
3) Habitat: Sometimes, you can find Vespula sqamosa in urban areas such as parks and roads, disturbed areas too, but typically you can find Southern Yellowjacket in warmer weather locations such as forests. This Yellowjacket was found in a hardwood swamp area. It was on the wooden boardwalk near the swamp. This was near many pine trees too. 
4) Defining Characteristics: Southern Yellowjackets are in phylum Anthropoda because of the three dividing body parts: head, thorax, and abdomen. 
5) Interaction: They eat away at pests on crops or other plants

description:
Under the grave stone of Carrie Estell Mobley (Nov 19, 1892-Sept 17, 1957). The epitaph says:
"In memory of our beloved mother
We do not know the pain you felt
We did not see you die
We only know you went away
And did not say goodbye
[some religious stuff]
Her children
[4 names]"

What a weird epitaph. None of the 4 children knew the pain she felt, saw her die, or got to say goodbye? they sure make it sound like they were estranged, and to me it sounds a little resentful. It says "our beloved mother" though, so it's just very confusing to me. Is the pain they refer to due to illness? or is it related to psychological pain, maybe of the estrangement? Was this a suicide? that makes the most sense. Maybe she was suffering from depression, withdrew from family and friends, and committed suicide alone and without leaving a note. Were they being deliberately cryptic to avoid the stigma?
We may never know... I couldn't find any details about her after a very quick search.
